title: Module 1: Introduction to PLC and industrial automation

lessons.c:
A PLC (programmable logic controller) is a rugged industrial computer. It reads inputs, runs a stored program and switches outputs, over and over, many times a second.

Unlike an office PC, it is built for dust, heat, vibration and electrical noise, and it responds in predictable, repeatable time.
lessons.x: On a bottling machine, a sensor detects a bottle (input), the program decides the bottle is in position, and the PLC opens the filling valve (output).
lessons.ex: List three machines you have seen that probably use a PLC. For each, name one input and one output.
q: Reads inputs, runs a program and controls outputs
A PLC reads inputs, executes its program and updates outputs.
Which of these is an input?
Sensors send signals into the PLC. Lamps and coils are driven by outputs.
Why is a PLC used instead of a normal PC on a machine?
It is built for harsh environments and predictable timing
Rugged hardware and predictable timing are what industrial control needs.
A push button wired to a PLC is:
A button sends a signal to the PLC, so it is an input.

lessons.c:
PLCs replaced wall-sized relay panels. Changing the logic no longer means rewiring, you edit the program and download it.

They are reliable, modular, easy to troubleshoot with online monitoring, and they speak standard industrial networks.
lessons.x: A factory needs a second conveyor speed. With relays that meant new wiring. With a PLC it is a program change.
lessons.ex: Write two reasons a factory would choose a PLC over relay logic for a new machine.
q: A main advantage over relay panels is:
Logic changes by editing the program
Editing software is far faster than rewiring.
Online monitoring helps because it lets you:
See live values while the machine runs
Seeing live signals makes faults quicker to find.
You add input and output cards as the machine grows
Modules can be added to match the machine.
Adding a new interlock condition is easiest by:
An interlock is just more logic in the program.
PLCs suit factories because they are:
Reliability in harsh conditions is the main reason.

lessons.c:
A PLC has a CPU that runs the program, memory, a power supply, input modules, output modules and communication interfaces.

Input modules turn field signals such as 24 V DC into data. Output modules turn program results into signals that drive actuators. In Beckhoff systems, EtherCAT I/O terminals play this role.
lessons.x: A limit switch closes, the input terminal reports TRUE, the CPU runs the logic, and an output terminal switches a 24 V relay.
lessons.ex: Draw a block diagram: sensor, input module, CPU, output module, actuator.
q: Convert field signals into data for the CPU
They bring real-world signals into the PLC.
Which of these is an actuator?
An actuator is driven by an output and acts on the process.
Send CPU results out to actuators
They convert program results into real signals.

lessons.c:
A PLC repeats a loop forever: read inputs, run the program, write outputs, then housekeeping and communication. One pass is a scan, often a few milliseconds.

Because the whole program runs each cycle, a signal shorter than the scan can be missed, and outputs only change at the end of the scan.
lessons.x: A conveyor sensor sees a box. On the next scan the program reads TRUE and the diverter output is set at the end of that scan.
lessons.code:
PROGRAM MAIN
VAR
  bSensor   : BOOL;   // input
  bDiverter : BOOL;   // output
  nScans    : UDINT;
END_VAR

nScans := nScans + 1;  // runs once every scan
bDiverter := bSensor;
lessons.ex: In TwinCAT online mode, watch nScans for ten seconds and estimate how many scans happen per second.
q: What is the correct scan order?
Write outputs, read inputs, run program
Read inputs, run program, write outputs
Inputs are read first, then logic runs, then outputs are written.
How often does the scan repeat?
The scan loops for as long as the PLC runs.
A pulse much shorter than the scan time may be:
If it starts and ends between two reads, the PLC never sees it.
In the code above, nScans increases:
The program body executes once each scan.
Scan time is the time for:
One full pass through the cycle
It is the duration of one complete loop.

lessons.c:
PLCs run packaging lines, conveyors, pumping stations, robot cells, lifts and process plants.

The pattern is the same everywhere: sense the process, decide with logic, act on the process, and report to operators.
lessons.x: In a water tank, a level sensor starts the pump at low level and stops it at high level, with an alarm if it runs too long.
lessons.ex: Pick a machine you know. Write its inputs, its outputs and one rule such as IF low level THEN pump ON.
q: Which is a typical PLC application?
Conveyors and sorting are classic PLC jobs.
Inputs sense, logic decides, outputs act.
In the water tank, the level sensor is:
It sends a signal into the PLC.
Actuators such as pumps are driven by outputs.
An alarm if the pump runs too long is:
Alarms and timeouts are just more program logic.
